blocks.text: Introducing Replit Missions
Agent swarms plan, build, test, and iterate toward the results you want, within the budget and boundaries you set.

inlines.text: Agent swarms plan, build, test, and iterate toward the results you want, within the budget and boundaries you set.

blocks.text: Published:
The Replit Team

Today, we’re launching Replit Missions to help your teams take on the complex work they haven't had time or capacity for: winning more enterprise customers, improving product performance, or replacing legacy software. You define the outcome, and Replit coordinates a swarm of agents to plan, build, test, and iterate toward it within the budget and boundaries you set.

inlines.text: Today, we’re launching Replit Missions to help your teams take on the complex work they haven't had time or capacity for: winning more enterprise customers, improving product performance, or replacing legacy software. You define the outcome, and Replit coordinates a swarm of agents to plan, build, test, and iterate toward it within the budget and boundaries you set.

blocks.text: At Replit, we wanted to explore bringing application monitoring in-house to reduce costs and gain more control. We gave Missions the goal of building DataCat, a platform we could customize and run on our own infrastructure. In two days, within a $3,000 budget, a swarm of agents built dashboards, alerts, and application tracing, then tested the platform against measurable performance and reliability goals.

blocks.text: Start with complex work you don’t have the capacity for

blocks.text: You can start with a mission like “win our first 10 paying enterprise customers.” You don’t need to decide upfront which industries to target, which buyers to reach, or which customer problem to solve first. Finding and evaluating those approaches is part of the work you delegate.

blocks.text: During setup, Missions asks questions to define success. What counts as an enterprise customer for your business? Do paid pilots count toward the first 10, or does success mean signed annual contracts above a minimum value? Your answers shape which accounts the mission prioritizes and how it measures results.

inlines.text: Stay in control of the budget and boundaries

blocks.text: Your Missions agreement sets the spending limit and which actions require your permission. You also agree on acceptable tradeoffs, such as offering paid pilots or discounts on annual contracts.

blocks.text: Agent swarms give Missions the capacity to explore multiple solutions at once, share insights, and build on each other’s discoveries. For a problem like performance optimization, agents test different implementations in parallel, use shared findings to refine their approaches, and work together to validate correctness as they identify faster solutions.

inlines.text: Agent swarms give Missions the capacity to explore multiple solutions at once, share insights, and build on each other’s discoveries. For a problem like performance optimization, agents test different implementations in parallel, use shared findings to refine their approaches, and work together to validate correctness as they identify faster solutions.

blocks.text: We put this to the test across 13 representative benchmark tasks using NumPy. Agents explored alternative implementations, optimized memory access patterns, and validated correctness automatically. With Auto (Max), a single agent achieved speedups of up to 4×. A 16-agent swarm reached 17×, and a 32-agent swarm reached 19×. Auto (Power) showed the same pattern: 2×, 7×, and 9×, respectively.

blocks.text: Building DataCat: our own application monitoring platform with Missions

inlines.text: Building DataCat: our own application monitoring platform with Missions

blocks.text: We used Missions to build DataCat, an application monitoring platform we can run and customize ourselves. In 2 days, with a $3,000 budget, Missions built a working platform with dashboards, alerts, and application tracing from goals our team set in the Mission Contract, then tested it against measurable performance and reliability goals.

inlines.text: We used Missions to build DataCat, an application monitoring platform we can run and customize ourselves. In 2 days, with a $3,000 budget, Missions built a working platform with dashboards, alerts, and application tracing from goals our team set in the Mission Contract, then tested it against measurable performance and reliability goals.

blocks.text: Missions also built DataCat’s own agent, which collects monitoring data from each server, and its tracing libraries. DataCat can run independently of the original platform’s agent and libraries.

inlines.text: Missions also built DataCat’s own agent, which collects monitoring data from each server, and its tracing libraries. DataCat can run independently of the original platform’s agent and libraries.

blocks.text: To test whether DataCat could help diagnose a failure, we deliberately introduced a database bug. DataCat raised an alert in 38 seconds, beating our 60-second target, and traced the failure to the exact database query and its logs.

inlines.text: To test whether DataCat could help diagnose a failure, we deliberately introduced a database bug. DataCat raised an alert in 38 seconds, beating our 60-second target, and traced the failure to the exact database query and its logs.

blocks.text: The mission also built sample applications for a three-hour load test. DataCat stored 26 million records of application activity and 4.4 million log entries with no data lost, while searches and alerts kept running. All 36 data-correctness checks and 15 alert-reliability checks passed.

inlines.text: The mission also built sample applications for a three-hour load test. DataCat stored 26 million records of application activity and 4.4 million log entries with no data lost, while searches and alerts kept running. All 36 data-correctness checks and 15 alert-reliability checks passed.

blocks.text: The mission compared its monitoring code with the original platform’s tracing library and agent. In matched Node.js tests, the application handled more requests with less monitoring-related processor overhead. DataCat’s agent also used less memory and made logs searchable sooner.

inlines.text: The mission compared its monitoring code with the original platform’s tracing library and agent. In matched Node.js tests, the application handled more requests with less monitoring-related processor overhead. DataCat’s agent also used less memory and made logs searchable sooner.

blocks.text: We then compared DataCat with a monitoring platform built with the same initial prompt using /goal in Claude Code. DataCat accepted all data types from the original platform’s agent (logs, metrics, host data and traces), while the Claude Code build accepted logs only. DataCat passed more API compatibility checks and took in traces and metrics faster. The Claude Code build covered more product areas and took in logs faster. The table below summarizes the results.

blocks.text: Put your ambition to work

Missions continues to impress us with the range of goals it can take on. On E-Commerce Bench, an agent starts with ¥100,000 and runs online stores for a simulated year, choosing suppliers, avoiding scams, and setting prices. In a single run, Missions grew that to ¥4.82 million, roughly 48 times the starting money, a state-of-the-art result more than three times the best on the public leaderboard.
